US Agencies Forced Down a Drone Over White Sands After Suspected Surveillance Flight
Monday, 31 August 2026, 13:20

The entrance to White Sands Missile Range near White Sands, New Mexico, photographed on February 21, 2024. Valerie Macon/AFP/Getty Images

A drone’s five-day intrusion over a restricted US missile range triggered an unusually broad response and raised questions about hidden surveillance.

In spring 2025, U.S. agencies intercepted a quadcopter that had violated the restricted airspace over White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico for approximately five days. The drone’s flight path suggested it may have been conducting reconnaissance of the military facility.

Based on data from CNN

The operation involved the U.S. Army, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Pentagon unit that analyzes unidentified anomalous phenomena. Electronic warfare measures forced the drone to land in a parking lot.

A Camper Van and Chinese Nationals Near a Military Base

At the same time, law enforcement officers were monitoring several Chinese nationals near White Sands. They arrived in the United States, rented a Mercedes camper van, and drove across the country to the missile range.

Separately, officials identified a Chinese woman who drove a rental car to White Sands National Park and remained there after it closed. The group in the camper van was detained by military personnel and later handed over to federal authorities. The woman was fined and released.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation suspected that the detained individuals could be linked to Chinese intelligence. Their subsequent fate has not been disclosed.

Claims that China is engaged in espionage are entirely without factual basis or evidence and are nothing more than unfounded speculation and sensational exaggeration.

– Spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy

Helicopters and a Drone Chase Over White Sands

The incident in spring 2025 was not the first time a suspicious drone had appeared over the military facility. In the fall of 2024, border agents pursued a similar drone over White Sands for about 56 kilometers, deploying helicopters and their own unmanned aircraft.

After the aircraft crossed the border into Mexico, the pursuit was called off. U.S. officials emphasize that not all illegal drone flights show signs of espionage. Drones are also launched by hobbyists, tourists, and criminal groups, which may use them to transport drugs.

Laser Systems Against Drones and Risks for the United States

The availability of inexpensive drones has made protecting U.S. military bases and critical infrastructure a separate challenge. For a long time, no agency had clearly defined responsibility for responding to such threats.

Following a series of incidents, U.S. Northern Command began coordinating responses to small drones appearing over military bases. The Pentagon is expanding its arsenal of countermeasures, including laser systems, high-powered microwave systems, and electronic warfare tools.

At the same time, the use of such technologies has already caused problems. In February, the airspace over El Paso was closed because of a poorly coordinated test of a laser system. Later, the military mistakenly shot down a U.S. Customs and Border Protection drone with a laser.

New Powers to Combat Drones

In 2026, the U.S. Congress expanded the powers of the Central Intelligence Agency, state authorities, and local police to force down drones that may threaten critical sites.

Counterintelligence specialists acknowledge that establishing a direct link between a specific drone flight and Chinese intelligence services is extremely difficult. In 2024, Chinese national Yinpiaо Zhou was detained for flying a drone over Vandenberg Space Force Base during the launch of a military satellite.

Zhou was sentenced to four months in federal prison for violating restricted airspace rules. U.S. officials believe that drone defense systems are gradually improving, but military facilities and critical infrastructure in the United States remain vulnerable.
